title: Chapter XLI

teacherSummary.text: Lydia is invited to Brighton by Mrs. Forster. Elizabeth warns her father of the danger; Mr. Bennet lets Lydia go to keep peace. Elizabeth sees Wickham again and hints she knows the truth.

words.sentence: If you, my dear father, will not take the trouble of checking her exuberant spirits, and of teaching her that her present pursuits are not to be the business of her life, she will soon be beyond the reach of amendment.
It was not in her nature, however, to increase her vexations, by dwelling on them.
Such squeamish youths as cannot bear to be connected with a little absurdity, are not worth a regret.
She had even learnt to detect, in the very gentleness which had first delighted her, an affectation and a sameness to disgust and weary.
Such were the kind of lamentations resounding perpetually through Longbourn-house.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Lydia will never be easy till she has exposed herself in some public place or other” slowly and put it in my own words: Mr. Bennet says Lydia will never be easy until she embarrasses herself in public, and Brighton will cost the family little. Next, craft. I notice his cool, cynical reasoning, which treats disgrace as inevitable. The strongest word is “exposed”: it predicts the disgrace he does nothing to prevent. Then, effect. Why does Mr. Bennet let Lydia go to Brighton? My answer: Mr. Bennet lets Lydia go to Brighton because he is lazy and wants peace at home, despite Elizabeth's warning; this failure leads directly to the elopement.
